why: Shorter: cuts the backstory paragraphs and the 'I used to think of being wrong as failure' title (framing/duty-free, fewer words wins); A's title states the point directly.
Author's own call (git-3ba7c052-44): 'a guess that happens to compile' puts the student's work down; B describes what the test does instead.
Cuts the trailing clause 'the shape the whole map has had from the start', a low-value closer and a course-about-itself remark; shorter wins.
Cuts the forward hint about Module 4 ('Module 4 will tell Claude…, that explicit list is the lesson'), which is a what's-coming-next line; B states the practice directly.
Shorter wins when the difference is a removed sentence; B's added narration of the agent's steps is a low-value restatement, and it recites what the agent does rather than what the student does.

B opens on the action ('Ask these one at a time') in fewer words; A's added line 'Three plain questions, one at a time, on the screen. Watch the tool list come back rather than typing along' repeats the previous sentence and makes the student passive, against the shorter-wins and never-passive rules.
Author's own KEPT text; B has passive/patronizing 'Nobody can hand you' and 'gift you haven't given yet', which he rejected.
Shorter wins: A's added closer 'Three modules in, this is your practice now' is a low-value restatement/closing sentence that the author cuts.

Verb precision: 'Check what Claude proposes' implies checking all of it; 'Read' is also all-of-it but the taste rule prefers a precise act, and neither says spot-check; B's 'Read' is the more literal act, A's 'Check' repeats the implied-exhaustive verb, so slight edge B but weak
Plain descriptive title that opens on the point; A's title 'Errors stack until a check resets them' is wordier and the shorter version wins when only a clause is removed
A is shorter and plain; B's 'written as an ADR' adds words, though the ADR acronym is kept in both. A cut-the-extra-clause call, but marginal.
'context window' repeats the next bullet's term; no rule or past call clearly favors either, and the difference is one word.
Matches the author's cut 'The lead-in previewed its own prompt; now it names the action' (same slide, same text): shorter, opens on the action.
Matches the tn-good-and-bad-work call: B's 'which one you get depends on...' makes the student passive and is wordier; A is shorter and names the LLM as actor.
Cuts 'and gives you the floor' and 'Swap a file path' (shorter wins when a clause or sentence is removed); 'committed change' is a coined term, 'alternative' says what it is.
B's 'One sentence buys the time back' is a clever closing kicker after the point is made; cut it.
Shorter wins when a whole sentence is removed; 'The agent works with exactly what you've given it' is a low-value restatement/closer.
Bolding the lead sentence of every bullet adds noise and weight to the third bullet; the author's cuts favour fewer, plainer words and the arc line is not worth emphasising.
